candidate.blueprint_locator: Management of Care — Advocacy and Client Rights
candidate.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — informed refusal and client rights
candidate.educational_objective: Apply client-rights principles to informed refusal by a capable adult and support a safe-as-feasible transition plan.

options.A: Respect the informed refusal after ensuring options and foreseeable consequences were discussed, document the discussion, and provide the safest feasible follow-up plan.
options.B: Prevent the client from leaving until the recommended treatment is completed because the healthcare team believes discharge is unsafe.
options.C: Treat the wish to leave as proof of incapacity and detain the client until a psychiatric evaluation authorizes discharge.
options.D: Ask the client to sign a refusal form before discussing alternatives or consequences because the signature alone completes informed refusal.

candidate.rationale: A capable adult may refuse recommended care. The nurse should support an informed refusal process: make sure relevant options and consequences are explained, document the discussion, and reduce harm with feasible follow-up. Capacity is not lost merely because the client chooses differently from the team, and a form is not a substitute for informed discussion.
candidate.source_claim_supported: A patient has rights concerning informed participation and refusal; capable refusal requires communication/documentation rather than automatic detention.
candidate.source_document_title: 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; 42 CFR 482.13 Patient Rights / CMS hospital guidance

candidate.source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN); Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)
candidate.source_version_date: NCSBN effective April 2026; CMS guidance QSO-24-10-Hospitals issued 2024-04-01
candidate.stem: An adult with decision-making capacity understands the recommended inpatient treatment and its risks but insists on leaving the hospital. What is the best response?
